source.title: Data Mixing Optimization for Supervised Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models
source.authors: Yuan Li; Zheng-Zhong Liu; E. Xing

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests the power-law form in the new setting of supervised fine-tuning, fitting loss against fine-tuning data and reporting validation-loss results across data budgets.
record.gate_note: The paper tests fine-tuning data scaling, not pretraining loss scaling in parameter count or compute. Its domain-weight and downstream-task results are included only where they bear on fine-tuning loss scaling or the relationship between validation loss and downstream performance. The paper’s discussion of other studies’ scaling results is not treated as evidence.
record.test_reason: This is a data-mixing method paper. It takes the fine-tuning power law L = C·|D|^-β + E from Zhang et al. (2024) as given and adds an effective-transfer term. It fits five parameters per domain from five perturbation runs spanning only 1/3n to 3n (one order of magnitude, one model, Llama3.2-3B), and gives no goodness-of-fit or comparison with alternative functional forms. What it evaluates is how its own optimized weights compare with grid search (Tables 7, 8) and with baselines (Tables 3, 4, 10, 11). The across-budget PPL drops in Table 7 mix changing data budgets, changing mixtures and changing step counts, and no power law is fitted to them. So the paper relies on the scaling law as a tool and reports its method's performance. It does not test whether the power-law form holds in SFT (V5) or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that their loss parameterization (an SFT data-scaling power law plus transferred effective data) yields near-optimal mixtures, with per-domain PPL on average 0.66% above grid search. They also find that reweighting Tulu3 improves both validation loss and downstream averages, while for Orca, lower validation loss does not translate into better downstream results.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than testing pretraining loss against parameter count, training tokens or compute, the paper models SFT validation loss using effective data transferred between domains and a fine-tuning data power law; it optimizes domain mixture weights.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted loss parameters differ across the tested domains. Optimal domain weights vary with data budget, and the paper reports that validation-loss reductions do not consistently translate to downstream improvements for Orca.

fits_no_version.finding: For Orca reweighting, the mixture with the lowest SFT validation PPL does not have the best downstream average. For Llama3.1-70B, Ours has PPL 1.643 and score 54.8, while Original has 1.666 and 57.2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SFT validation loss across data mixtures may not predict downstream performance when validation and test distributions differ.

fits_no_version.finding: The SFT loss fits for IF, math and code on Llama3.2-3B give small exponents βi of 0.043–0.051, and loss-minimising domain weights shift with data budget.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitted SFT data-scaling exponents differ by domain, and the optimal mixture depends on scale.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025)
record.problems: The direct fine-tuning data perturbation fit is reported for one model, Llama3.2-3B, over a limited range of data-size ratios. The broader budget comparisons involve changing optimized mixtures as well as changing data budgets, so they are not an isolated test of a single loss curve. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 8 per-domain PPL results for the four models and three budgets, and other dataset-reweighting PPL and downstream results, were not entered as separate rows; the 60-row limit was not reached, but these were omitted as secondary results beyond the direct fine-tuning scaling test and the reported Orca loss/downstream discrepancy.

untested.parts: All of it: pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All of it. The fitted SFT law is used to choose weights, not checked against much larger runs' loss.
All of it: no allocation between parameters and tokens.
All of it: no shape comparisons.
Whether the power-law form holds for SFT data scaling. The form is assumed, fitted over a 9x range on one model, and no fit quality or alternative form is reported.
All of it: downstream results are compared across mixtures, not across scale or pretraining loss.
All of it: no comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: I reclassified the record from tests/T3 to uses_without_test/T4 and dropped its V5 supports label. The power law is borrowed from Zhang et al. (2024) and assumed; the exponents are parameters of the method. Table 7's budget trends conflate budget, mixture and training steps, and compare the paper's method with grid search. The paper is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Pretraining loss scaling in parameters, tokens or compute when other factors are not bottlenecks.
No power-law fit on small runs is used to predict losses of much larger runs.
Does not test compute-optimal allocation between parameter count and token count, or their growth with compute.
Does not compare architecture depth, width or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

Tests fine-tuning data scaling in SFT, but not other modalities, repeated-data effects as a scaling-law question, or transfer scaling. The perturbation range is limited to data-size ratios 1/3, 1/2, 1, 2 and 3.
Does not test downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss or scale. It reports a related comparison using SFT validation PPL and downstream scores.
Does not compare fitting methods or parameter-counting, schedule, data or other setup choices to test whether fitted laws or exponents depend on them.

relation.reason: Section 3.3 adopts the fine-tuning scaling relationship from Zhang et al. (2024); the reported comparisons evaluate mixture optimization. SFT validation PPL versus downstream scores across mixtures does not test V6's scale or pretraining-loss relationship.

tranche.reason: The study adopts a cited fine-tuning power law to construct a data-mixture optimization method and evaluates the resulting mixtures. It does not independently test the catalog's scaling-law versions.

source_check.notes: Appendix E.4's prose overstates the Qwen2.5-32B comparison: Table 10 reports equal average PPL for Ours and Equal I. The pack's one-model characterization applies to the Section 4 illustration; Section 5 evaluates multiple models.

statements.correction: Orca, Llama3.1-70B: Ours average PPL 1.643, downstream average 54.8; Original average PPL 1.668, downstream average 57.2.
statements.problem: The Original-mixture PPL is incorrect; the model, Ours values and Original downstream average are correct.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Llama3.2-3B SFT domain-data perturbations and tested models trained at 5M, 20M and 200M tokens
reader_labels.reason: The fitted loss model has positive reported power-law exponents for all three domains (r1–r3); the perturbation figure is described as showing lower domain loss with increased domain data (r4–r6), and overall validation PPL decreases across the reported budgets for the tested models (r7–r30). The evidence supports this form in the tested SFT settings, not across several orders of magnitude.
